::: {.lead}
Today you practise what the teacher explained, like in a lab. Each
experiment has two parts. **Part A** is on the computer, in the browser and
OneDrive. **Part B** is on your phone or on a simulator of the interactive
lesson: on paper, scan its QR code; on the screen, click its link. After
each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy your key results
into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with a browser, your university account, and
  your phone.
- **No lab computer today?** Do Part B of each experiment on your phone. Do
  Part A later on any computer, in the browser at `office.com`.
- **Never** type your password on a page of this course, and never save it
  on a lab computer.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers at
  once.

## Experiment 1 · One account, one sign-in

**The idea:** your **account** is your user name, your password and your
data. **Authentication** means that you prove that the account is yours:
you type your password, and often a code comes to your phone. With **single
sign-on**, you sign in one time, and all university services open. The risk:
a stolen password opens everything. On a lab computer, never save your
password, lock the screen when you leave (Windows key + L), and press
**Sign out** when you finish.

**Aim:** see single sign-on at work, and keep your account safe on a lab
computer.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the browser (the lab computer)**
:::

1. Open `office.com` and sign in with your university account. Then open
   **Outlook**, and after it **OneDrive**, from the list of apps. Does one
   of them ask for your password again?

   {{< record "Password asked again? … ; this is called …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **No.** You signed in one time, and e-mail and OneDrive both open: this
   is **single sign-on**. It saves time, but a stolen password opens every
   service.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You sign in at `office.com`. Then Outlook and OneDrive open without your
   password. What is this called?

   - [x] single sign-on

     Why: One sign-in opens all the university services.

   - [ ] authentication

     Why: Authentication is proving that the account is yours, when you sign in.

   - [ ] cloud storage

     Why: Cloud storage keeps your files on the Internet; it is not the sign-in.
   :::

2. Press **Windows key + L**. What do you see? Then open the computer again
   (it asks for the password of the computer).

   {{< record "After Windows key + L, I see" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The **lock screen**. Your work stays open, but nobody can use it until
   the password is typed again. Lock the screen when you leave the computer
   for a minute.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You leave a lab computer for one minute. What do you do?

   - [x] Lock the screen with Windows key + L.

     Why: The screen locks, and your account stays safe.

   - [ ] Close the browser.

     Why: Closing the browser does not always sign you out.

   - [ ] Nothing: one minute is very short.

     Why: In one minute, another person can read or send your e-mails.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On your phone** (no computer? start here)
:::

3. On your phone, open `office.com` in the browser (or the Outlook app) and
   sign in with your university account. Open your e-mail. Do you see the
   same e-mails as on the lab computer?

   {{< record "The same e-mails? … ; because …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Yes**, for example the e-mails from the university. It is one account:
   your user name, your password and your data, on every device. On your
   own phone you may stay signed in; on a lab computer, press **Sign out**
   when you finish.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You sign in on your phone with your university account. What do you
   see in your e-mail?

   - [x] The same e-mails as on the lab computer.

     Why: It is one account: your user name, your password and your data, on every device.

   - [ ] Other e-mails: the phone has its own account.

     Why: You signed in with the same university account, so you see the same data.

   - [ ] No e-mails: e-mail works only on a computer.

     Why: Your account works on every device, after you sign in.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Folders, paths and good file names

**The idea:** a **file** is one saved piece of work. A **folder** keeps files
and other folders: folders in folders make a tree. The **path** is the full
address of a file, for example
`C:\Users\Sara\Documents\Courses\Digital-Skills\unit-01\cv.docx`. The
**extension** after the last dot shows the type: `.docx` Word, `.xlsx`
Excel, `.pptx` PowerPoint, `.jpg` a photo, `.exe` a program. A good file name
says what it is, has no spaces, has the date as year-month-day, and has a
version (`v01`, `v02`), never "final".

**Aim:** make your course folders, and save a file with a good name.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (OneDrive in the browser)**
:::

1. Open **OneDrive** from `office.com`. Click **New** (or **Add new**) →
   **Folder** and make the folder **Courses**. Open it and make
   **Digital-Skills** in it, then **unit-01** in that one. Look at the line
   of folder names at the top.

   {{< record "The line at the top shows" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **My files › Courses › Digital-Skills › unit-01**: the path of your
   folder, from the top of the tree. Each folder is inside the one before
   it.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   Put the folders in order, from the top of the tree to the folder of this
   unit.

   1. My files
   2. Courses
   3. Digital-Skills
   4. unit-01

   Why: Each folder is inside the one before it: the path goes from the top of the tree down to unit-01.
   :::

2. In **unit-01**, click **New** → **Word document**. Type your name and
   today's date. Then give the file a good name (click its name at the top,
   or **Rename** in OneDrive): the date as year-month-day, what it is and a
   version, for example `2026-10-26_first-file_v01`. Word adds `.docx`.

   {{< record "My file name" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good name, for example **2026-10-26_first-file_v01.docx**: the date
   first, a word that says what it is, the version and no spaces. Word added
   the extension `.docx`.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Sara's CV was made on 26 October 2026. It is the first version. Which
   name follows the four rules?

   - [x] `2026-10-26_cv_v01.docx`

     Why: The date first (year-month-day), what it is, the version and no spaces.

   - [ ] `New Document (3).docx`

     Why: It does not say what the file is.

   - [ ] `cv final 26-10-2026.docx`

     Why: It has spaces, the word final, and the day first.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-01/sims/folder-lab.html" poster="../../week-01/sims/folder-lab.png" title="Folder Lab: folders and good file names" >}}

3. In **Folder Lab**, part 1: make the folders **Courses**, **Digital-Skills**
   and **unit-01** in Documents. Look at the address line. Then, in part 2,
   give the three files good names.

   {{< record "The address line in unit-01 shows" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **C:\\Users\\Sara\\Documents\\Courses\\Digital-Skills\\unit-01**: the
   path of the folder. In part 2, good names are for example
   `2026-10-26_cv_v01.docx` and `2026-11-12_english-talk_v03.pptx`.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   In Folder Lab, `final final.pptx` is Sara's English talk of 12 November
   2026, third version. Which name is good?

   - [x] `2026-11-12_english-talk_v03.pptx`

     Why: It has the date first, what it is, the version and no spaces.

   - [ ] `english talk final.pptx`

     Why: It has spaces and the word final, and no date or version.

   - [ ] `2026-11-12_english-talk_v03`

     Why: A file keeps its extension: .pptx shows that PowerPoint opens it.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · Cloud storage, sync and backup

**The idea:** **cloud storage** (OneDrive, Google Drive) keeps your files on
the Internet: you open them on any device after you sign in. **Sync** keeps
the same files on all your devices. It also copies your mistakes: delete a
file in one place, and it is gone everywhere. The **recycle bin** of the
cloud keeps deleted files for some days. A **backup** is an extra copy in a
separate place, for example a USB stick: a mistake does not reach it.

**Aim:** get a deleted file back, and see why sync is not a backup.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (OneDrive in the browser)**
:::

1. In OneDrive, open **unit-01**. Select your Word file and click
   **Delete**. Then open the **Recycle bin** (on the left side), select the
   file and click **Restore**. Open **unit-01** again.

   {{< record "Where I found the file … ; where it is now …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   In the **Recycle bin** of OneDrive. After **Restore**, the file is back
   in **unit-01**. The recycle bin keeps deleted files for some days only.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You delete a file in OneDrive by mistake. Where do you look first?

   - [x] in the recycle bin of OneDrive

     Why: The cloud keeps deleted files there for some days.

   - [ ] on your phone

     Why: Sync copies the delete: the file is gone on the phone too.

   - [ ] nowhere: a deleted file is gone at once

     Why: The recycle bin keeps it for some days.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="../../week-01/sims/sync-lab.html" poster="../../week-01/sims/sync-lab.png" title="Sync Lab: sync, recycle bin and backup" >}}

2. In **Sync Lab**, do the five missions. In mission 4 you delete the photo
   and empty the recycle bin. Where is a copy of the photo then?

   {{< record "After mission 4, a copy is" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Only on the USB stick at home**: the backup. Sync deleted the photo on
   every device, and the empty recycle bin has nothing. Sync is not a
   backup.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   In Sync Lab, you delete photo.jpg on the lab computer. Is it still on the
   phone?

   - [x] No: sync deletes it on every device.

     Why: Sync copies every change, a delete too.

   - [ ] Yes: the phone keeps its own copy.

     Why: The phone is synced, so the delete reaches it too.
   :::
